posts.note: Inauguration-day essay on white privilege, policing and mental illness. Mostly present-tense analysis and cited statistics; three vague rhetorical future claims logged for recall.

Parody coronation address by 'President Richard III' (Trump as Richard III). All promises are in a fictional voice; two with real-policy shadows (ending war, rounding up 'Chad' immigrants) logged with sincere=false. Pure absurdist jokes (no more clouds, R. Kelly to head the NEA, Stacys allocated to incels, marrying Lady Anne) not logged.
OCD explainer. Epidemiological figures such as '14% of people with OCD will attempt suicide' are cited statistics, not forecasts.

Declared satire: a 'victory lap' over UnitedHealth CEO Andrew Witty's vow to reduce prior authorization. Several ironic future claims logged with sincere=false; the unconfirmed insider layoff tip and the Google News indexing claim read as sincere. 'More lawsuits, as I predicted' refers to an earlier call already realized, not logged.

Peer-to-peer review transcript with a UHC medical director. The reviewer's 'will not approve' lines are third-party statements of present coverage policy, not forecasts; the author's 'I am appealing it yet again' is an action, not a prediction.
Essay against celebrating the murder of the UnitedHealthcare CEO. Truisms ('it will never be cool to stop them in the moment') and the normative 'We will have to trust due process' not logged.
Macbeth parody on Vivek Ramaswamy's exit from DOGE. The joke that 2025 'has been declared the end of time' not logged.

Review of a UK matched-cohort study on life expectancy in adult ADHD. One general risk claim logged as borderline (forward_looking=false); the rest is study description and normative calls for public-health focus.
Republished 'classic' essay (author says he is giving grand rounds). Wishes ('I hope Sam Bankman-Fraud ends up punished legally') and counterfactuals not logged.
Historical essay on the 430 BC plague of Athens; one hedged pandemic-risk hint logged.
Satirical imagined Senate hearing about the newsletter itself; no forward-looking claims about the world.

statements.quote: Martin Luther King had a dream, and it will take longer to realize it.
statements.context: Closing section of an inauguration-day essay (2025-01-20) on white privilege, policing, guns and mental illness. The author asserts that MLK's dream of racial justice will take longer to realize, with no date given.
statements.note: Vague, undated rhetorical claim; likely unresolvable. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: White privilege will, eventually, turn on you , like a viper, the second you try to get in its way .
statements.context: Same essay. General claim that the system of white privilege will eventually harm even the white people who benefit from it, once they oppose it. Illustrated earlier with the example of a white grandparent whose grandchild is Black and mentally ill.
statements.note: Rhetorical generalization about a social system, not a dated event; borderline forecast.

statements.quote: We will all be judged by the content of our character; the question is only when .
statements.context: Final line of the essay, echoing MLK. Moral assertion that judgment on character will come at an unknown time; followed by a call to hold each other accountable now.
statements.note: Moral aphorism, likely unresolvable. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: There will be no more war, and because of it, we're gonna get to spend more time with ladies.
statements.context: Parody coronation address by 'President Richard III' (a Trump/Richard III mash-up) published the day after the 2025 inauguration. The character promises to abolish war, satirizing the new president's promises to end wars.
statements.note: Voiced by a parody character; satire of the incoming president's promises. No sincere expectation stated by the author.

statements.quote: There have been rumors that Chads are immigrants, they're not from here, and those Chads, they are going to be imprisoned. And then we're gonna round them up
statements.context: Same parody address. The character promises to imprison and round up 'Chads' framed as immigrants, a satire of mass-deportation promises.
statements.note: Voiced by a parody character; satire of mass-deportation promises. No sincere expectation stated by the author.

statements.quote: So we will see if this piece of information pans out. But it looks as if United has another reduction in force, on top of the several rounds they had in 2024.
statements.context: Breaking-news aside inserted just before publishing a satirical UnitedHealth piece. An unconfirmed 'UHC insider' tip (screenshot not in text) suggests UnitedHealth Group is running another round of layoffs after several rounds in 2024.
statements.note: Based on an unconfirmed insider tip; the claim is that a new UHC reduction in force is under way and will be confirmed.

statements.quote: I intend to take Andrew Witty at his word, and I do believe that they're gonna keep at that gap until it's closed
statements.context: Satirical 'victory lap' over a Managed Healthcare Executive report that UnitedHealth Group CEO Andrew Witty vowed to reduce prior authorization and close the gap in digital health interactions. The author ironically professes belief that UHC will keep at it until the gap is closed.
statements.note: Ironic, inside a declared satire. Underlying sincere reading is doubt that UHC's prior-authorization vow is fulfilled promptly.

statements.quote: it's the time scale that I'm not entirely clear on. It could take… Any amount of time… which might limit the immediacy of the relief individuals would feel?
statements.context: Immediately follows the ironic profession of belief in Witty's vow. The author's actual expectation: UHC's prior-authorization reduction has no stated timescale and may bring no immediate relief. He adds that Optum's podcast is titled 'Until It's Fixed', again with no timescale.
statements.note: Rhetorical question form inside a satire, but reads as the author's real skepticism about the speed of UHC prior-auth relief.

statements.quote: Andrew Witty, I salute you. Thank you for your Vow to change things for the better, I have no reason to believe that that's not exactly what's going to happen.
statements.context: Closing of the satire. Ironically asserts full confidence that Witty's vow to reduce prior authorization and change UnitedHealthcare for the better will be fulfilled.
statements.confidence_phrase: I have no reason to believe that that's not exactly what's going to happen
statements.note: Ironic; underlying sincere reading is skepticism that UHC changes its prior-authorization practices.

statements.quote: I presume we'll add more value-based contracting and the CPT codes for fMRI-guided accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation any day now?
statements.context: Final line of the satire. A rhetorical, ironic question implying UnitedHealthcare will not soon add value-based contracting or CPT codes for fMRI-guided accelerated TMS, the author's own clinical area.
statements.note: Rhetorical ironic question; underlying reading is doubt that UHC adds coverage or CPT codes for fMRI-guided accelerated TMS soon. Touches the author's own practice area (possible CONTROL).

statements.quote: every time I write anything about United healthcare, everybody who's got a Google news alert about it is gonna get my article in their inbox.
statements.context: The author notes that his newsletter is now indexed by Google News as a news source, and claims that every future article he writes about UnitedHealthcare will reach everyone with a Google News alert for the company.
statements.note: About the author's own newsletter (CONTROL candidate). Boastful tone inside a satire, but the indexing claim reads as sincere.

statements.quote: O.K., maybe there was an inauguration this week, which may impact public markets.
statements.context: Aside within the satire, conceding an 'unforeseen circumstance' other than the author's mockery that could explain UnitedHealth's share-price movement and earnings: the presidential inauguration may affect public markets.
statements.note: Ironic understatement in an aside; vague, low forecast value.

statements.quote: We should not fail to imagine what it's like to live under that kind of threat. It's gonna be true for a lot of people soon.
statements.context: Essay condemning those who cheered the murder of the UnitedHealthcare CEO and defending the dignity of health-plan employees, who a colleague at UnitedHealth says are receiving constant death threats. The author predicts that living under threat of violence will soon be true for many people.
statements.note: First sentence is normative; the second is the prediction. Referent ('that kind of threat') is threat of political violence.

statements.quote: Ironically, I'm probably also going to get death threats for saying even this.
statements.context: Same essay. The author predicts that he himself will receive death threats for defending the dignity and safety of UnitedHealth employees.
statements.note: About the author personally; self-referential and hard to verify.

statements.quote: It is a tale Told by an idiot, full of promises and vitriol, Reforming nothing.
statements.context: Macbeth 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow' parody marking Vivek Ramaswamy's departure from DOGE (the Department of Government Efficiency), where he was to cut 'unnecessary regulations'. The verse likens the regulatory-reform effort to a Theranos-style founder and concludes it reforms nothing.
statements.note: Parody verse (line breaks collapsed); reads as sincere cynicism that DOGE's deregulation push will accomplish nothing. Borderline sincere flag.

statements.quote: Our best luck to Mr. R. In whatever run for public office he chooses for himself in the great state of Ohio.
statements.context: Closing well-wish after Ramaswamy's exit from DOGE. Presupposes that Ramaswamy will run for public office in Ohio.
statements.note: Well-wish with an embedded expectation (a run for office in Ohio); no explicit prediction verb.

statements.quote: Yes, your ADHD medication might kill you. But, it's more likely your ADHD will kill you on it's own if left untreated. The deaths happen early, and the risks happen late.
statements.context: Summary of the author's earlier essay 'Is My ADHD Medication Killing Me?', restated in a post reviewing a UK matched-cohort study (O'Nions et al., 2025) that found 6.78 (men) and 8.64 (women) years of reduced life expectancy in adults with diagnosed ADHD. General risk claim: untreated ADHD is more likely to kill than stimulant medication.
statements.note: Borderline: general epidemiological risk claim restated from an earlier essay, not a forecast of a dated event. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: I really do think “Theranos” tech—what they actually built—is a hot opportunity for investors in health tech, if it weren’t for the obvious imprisoned-founder problem.
statements.context: Republished 'classic' essay titled 'Theranos Was a Good Investment [and still is!]'. The author asserts, explicitly not just as clickbait, that the technology Theranos actually built (a fingerstick single-test device) is undervalued and a hot opportunity for health-tech investors, absent the imprisoned-founder problem.
statements.note: Investment-thesis claim with an implicit forecast of value; title says Theranos 'still is' a good investment. Republished older essay.

statements.quote: don’t think this is not normal Silicon Valley behavior. It is. ... And it will continue till we demand otherwise
statements.context: Closing argument of the Theranos essay: fake-it-till-you-make-it and near-fraud are normal Silicon Valley behavior, and the author predicts this will continue until the public demands verification, for example a public ledger of startup finances and governance.
statements.note: Open-ended horizon, conditional on public demand. An image caption sits between the two joined parts. Republished older essay.

statements.quote: Invest your money somewhere safe, like by subscribing to this Substack. It’s guaranteed to be worth nothing to you, but leave you feeling ok
statements.context: Closing joke of the Theranos essay: subscribing to the newsletter is 'guaranteed' to be worth nothing financially but to leave readers feeling OK, unlike Theranos or FTX investors.
statements.note: Self-deprecating joke about the author's own newsletter (CONTROL); not a real expectation.

statements.quote: Unless of course, H5N1, Marburg, or some other fearsome plague rears its ugly head. We might be dragged back to our primeval state, yet again?
statements.context: Essay on the 430 BC plague of Athens and the collapse of social norms that Thucydides described, written 'for no particular reason'. The author hints that a new plague (H5N1, Marburg or another) could drag modern society back into the same fear-driven breakdown.
statements.note: Conditional, rhetorical-question form; the pandemic-risk hint is the sincere kernel of an otherwise historical essay.
